title: History of Lasem
content:
Lasem is an ancient city located on the northern coast of central Java. Geographically, Lasem's location on the northern coast makes this region very strategic. This allowed Lasem to develop as an economic center and become a stage for cultural diversity. Through an ethno-historical lens, we can deepen our understanding of the diverse lives of its people, as well as the cultural heritage that has been passed down from generation to generation.

Lasem is known as a city with a long history involving interactions between Javanese and Chinese cultures, as well as global cultural influences. At that time, social life in Lasem was characterized by the presence of a Chinese community that had settled for generations, blending with the local Javanese community. The relationship between these two communities was dynamic and mutually influential, seen from activities in public spaces such as markets and community events reflecting high tolerance and cooperation.

Lasem also became a unique center of cultural interaction, where Javanese and Chinese cultures influenced each other in various aspects of daily life. The architecture of houses, clothing, and arts in Lasem often reflected a blend of the two cultures. For example, Lasem batik motifs combine traditional Javanese elements with Chinese symbols such as dragons and phoenixes, while traditional ceremonies show dual influences from both cultures in certain celebrations.

Cultural interactions between the Javanese and Chinese in Lasem are also seen in social aspects such as intermarriage and language use. Intermarriages between Javanese and Chinese communities not only bound two families but also combined the traditions and customs of both cultures, enriching the local culture as a whole. The language used in Lasem reflects this interaction, with many speaking a mixed dialect that shows the community's openness to other cultural influences.

In terms of trade economy, Lasem was a vital trading center on the northern coast of Java. The presence of an active port allowed Lasem to become a meeting point for merchants from various countries, bringing in commodities such as spices, textiles, ceramics, and agricultural products traded for local goods. Chinese merchants played an important role in Lasem's economy, operating shops and participating in international trade.

The batik industry was also an important part of the local economy, with Lasem known as one of the producers of high-quality batik sold in local and international markets. The influence of maritime trade was very significant in the development of Lasem. The busy Lasem port brought various commodities from and to foreign countries, with ships from China, India, Arabia, and Europe frequently stopping at this port. Port infrastructure developed rapidly to support trading activities, making Lasem an important point in the international maritime trade network. This trade not only enriched the local economy but also brought in cultural and technological influences from outside, shaping the unique character of Lasem city which is harmonious and diverse.

title: History of Lasem Up To the 15th Century
content:
Not much information can be uncovered when talking about Lasem-Rembang before the period of Majapahit rule. However, the discovery of an ancient boat in Punjulharjo Village, estimated to date from the 7th century, reaffirms the existence of maritime life in the region (Purnawibawa, 2021). The Lasem-Rembang area might have evolved into a bustling port. Although the ancient boat was likely made by local people, it was used by Indo-Chinese (Champa) merchants. The boat may have been used to travel from the river mouth to the hinterland, considering the center of the kingdom at that time was probably located inland. Various commodities left behind (statues and daily life equipment) on the boat also indicate social-economic interactions between the Javanese and Indo-Chinese. It is estimated that since the 11th century, there has been a settlement of Chinese merchants who stayed and intermarried with the natives around the Lasem River (Handinoto, 2015), and it is even believed that part of the current Chinese community in Lasem are descendants of the crew from Admiral Zheng He's expedition in the 14th century who settled in Lasem (Unjiya, 2014).

In the 14th century, Majapahit began to establish its hegemony over Java. Lasem-Rembang became a vassal of Majapahit under an official holding the title of Bhre Lasem (Purnawibawa, 2021). In this period, Lasem, as described in the Carita Sejarah Lasem, was a comfortable, peaceful, and beautiful region. With a very strategic position, it is highly likely that Lasem (including Rembang), along with Gresik (Sedayu and Jaratan), were important areas for Majapahit's maritime strength (Purnawibawa, 2020). It is estimated that the shipyard during this period was located at the Kairingan (Kiringan) port. Meanwhile, the trading center was in the Regol Bay area, which was enlivened by inter-island and international trade activities (Unjiya, 2014). Up to the 15th century, the main location for building large-sized boats on the northern coast of Java is estimated to have been in Rembang and Cirebon (Manguin, 1993). This further strengthens the opinion that coastal communities in Rembang already possessed skills in boat-building technology.

If Lasem in the 14th-15th century was Majapahit's main port in Java, it is possible that Odorico do Pordenone, an Italian traveler, once visited the Lasem-Rembang area. Odorico is thought to have been in Java when Majapahit was under the leadership of King Jayanegara. Odorico closely observed the political economy of Majapahit. The Majapahit political bureaucracy was glimpsed by him. He felt the Javanese King had seven other kings under his supreme rule (Rush, 2012:2). If we look closely, it is possible that what he meant by the seven subordinate kings of the Majapahit king was the Bathara Sapta Prabu. In addition, the advisory council was also called by other names such as Sapta Raja, Mantri Agung, Kalawan Para Natha, Pohom Narendra, and Saptangga Raja (Yamin, 1962:91). Bathara Sapta Prabu was an advisory position to the king whose members were the ruling royal family (Yamin, 1962:87). When Jayanegara was in power, it is not yet known who was included in the Bathara Sapta Prabu circle, which was formed after Raden Wijaya passed away (Yamin, 1962:90). However, when Hayam Wuruk came to power, information on who the Bathara Sapta Prabu were can be known. In the Singasari Inscription of 1351, it is mentioned that the Bathara Sapta Prabu was headed by Tribuana Tungga Dewi (Yamin, 1962:88). Initially, Sapta Prabu consisted of seven people, namely King Hayam Wuruk, his parents, aunt and uncle, and two female siblings. However, the number of its members likely increased in 1354. Although the number changed to nine people, the name remained Bathara Sapta Prabu (Yamin, 1962:89). The nine people who became Bathara Sapta Prabu were King Hayam Wuruk as chairman of the council, Tribhuwana Tungga Dewi, Sri Kerta Wardhana, Dyah Wiyat Sri Raja Dewi, Sri Wijaya Rajasa, Bhre Lasem Duhitendu Dewi, Sri Rajasa Wardhana, Bhre Pajang, and Singa Wardana (Unjiya, 2014:24).

Another testimony from Odorico is the geography and commodities in Java. According to him, Java is the largest island in the world and is fully inhabited (Rush, 2012:2). Marco Polo also exclaimed the same thing. Polo (2019:24 & 250) stated that, according to veteran sailors, Java is the largest island in the world. Of course, this information is not entirely accurate and does not correspond to reality. Regarding commodities in Java, Odorico said that the ports in Java have cloves, cubeb, and nutmeg as well as all kinds of other spices, and also many types of food in large quantities. However, Java has no wine (Rush, 2012:2). Not much different, Polo (2019: 250) conveyed that Java is an island rich in commodities. They have pepper, nutmeg, cloves, as well as various types of spices found in the world. So many ships and merchants trade in Java and gain high trading profits. Ma Huan's work entitled Ying-yai Sheng-lan also provides information on commodities in Java. The Chinese traveler found various agricultural products such as rice, sesame, and soybeans. In addition, Java also produces sappanwood, diamonds, sandalwood, pepper, steel, and turtle shells (Groeneveldt, 2019:67). The availability of commodities in Java is certainly based on the demand for goods by foreign merchants. Chinese merchants, for example, really sought after black pepper. In addition, other foreign merchants also sought rice, beans, fennel, safflower dye, jamuju seeds, coriander seeds, wangkudu dye, salt, and sugar. Besides exported commodities, it turns out there are several commodities brought to Java such as ceramics, cloth, frankincense, swords, metals, coins, and slaves (Christie, 1998:352; Nufus, 2018).

Besides political bureaucracy and trade commodities, Odorico also mentioned his amazement at the Javanese palace. He stated that the Javanese King has a large and luxurious palace that is the most amazing. The palace has a wide and majestic staircase leading to the upper rooms, all steps alternately made of gold and silver. The entire inner wall is covered with gold plating, where images of knights are carved onto the gold plating. The knight images are adorned with a small crown decorated with various precious stones. The roof of the palace is made of pure gold and the entire lower rooms are covered and alternated with square-shaped plates made of gold and silver (Rush, 2012:2). The Javanese palace in question is likely the capital of Majapahit, namely Trowulan. As far as the studies conducted so far, experts still agree that the Majapahit capital was located there (Munandar, 2008). Regarding the description of the Majapahit palace, other information can be traced from Mpu Prapanca's description in the Nagarakrtagama (Riana, 2009) and Ma Huan in Ying-yai Sheng-lan (Groeneveldt, 2019:63-4). According to them, the Majapahit palace was surrounded by high red brick walls as high as three chang or spears and very thick. Nearby there was a post where soldiers stood guard. Their guard was very strict and layered. The main gate leading to the palace (palace complex) is located on the north side of the wall, in the form of a grand gate with large doors made of carved iron. In front of the north gate, there is a long building for the annual state officials' meeting, a market, and a sacred intersection. Entering the complex through the north gate is a square surrounded by sacred religious buildings. On the west side of this square is a pavilion surrounded by canals and pools where people bathe. At the southern end of the square are various houses built on terraced platforms, these houses are the residences of the palace servants. Another gate leads to a third square full of buildings and a large hall. This building is a waiting room for guests who will face the king. The king's palace complex is located on the east side of this square, in the form of several pavilions built on carved brick platforms, with large wooden pillars carved very finely and roofs decorated with clay ornaments.

Finally, Odorico also provided information regarding the geopolitical state of Asia. The Chinese Emperor or the Great Khan often waged wars with the King of Java. However, according to him, Chinese attacks were always successfully broken and repelled (Rush, 2012:2). Polo (2019:8) also provided similar information when describing Java. He said the Khan's forces had just lost in Java. Historically, the Chinese Emperor did send troops twice to Java. First, when he asked his diplomats to expect recognition from King Kertanegara. Second, Chinese troops came again with the intention of punishing Kertanegara who refused to submit to China. However, the Chinese troops could no longer find Kertanegara who was killed when Jayakatwang ravaged the Singasari palace. Raden Wijaya, who survived Jayakatwang's attack, then negotiated and agreed to attack Kediri together. Their alliance successfully wiped out Jayakatwang and his allies. Complacent about the victory they had achieved, the Chinese troops held a victory party. In a heavily drunken state, the Chinese troops were unprepared for a sudden attack by Raden Wijaya. Raden Wijaya successfully annihilated and expelled the Chinese troops. Residing in Tarik, Raden Wijaya then founded the Majapahit kingdom (Groeneveldt, 2019:40-48).

title: History of Lasem in the 16th Century
content:
Looking at Lasem from its geographical aspect, it is not surprising that in the early modern era, Lasem became an important area in the maritime trade sector. Being situated around Demak's territory was also a reason why the Lasem area became a connecting port to the hinterland for foreign merchants. To view the mobility of communication that occurred in Lasem in the 16th century, it is necessary to look at the power of Demak's influence following the fall of Majapahit's rule. Demak, which was oriented towards maritime strength, managed to establish good relations with Gresik, Tuban, and Lasem (Unjiya, 2014). This was because, during the late Majapahit era, these areas were a crucial part of Majapahit's defense and economy. In the 14th-15th century, Lasem was led by a Queen given the title Bhre Lasem. Javanese records mention that her real name was Duhitendu Dewi, a daughter of Wijaya Rajasa who married Dyah Wiyat, the sister of Tribhuana Tungga Dewi, Hayam Wuruk's mother. In this sense, Bhre Lasem was the cousin of King Hayam Wuruk. This signifies that Lasem held an important position for the Majapahit Kingdom. Therefore, looking at Lasem's past greatness, the Demak Kingdom's political move to control Lasem aimed to gain power both politically and geographically.

The ease of Demak having a relationship with Lasem was also caused by Islam entering Lasem in the early 15th century. Islam came to Lasem initially through the arrival of a merchant named Bi Nang Un (Rangkuti, 1997). Bi Nang Un was one of the crew members of Admiral Zheng He's Ship. Bi Nang Un wanted to settle in Lasem to spread Islam among the natives. Bi Nang Un anchored in Bonang bringing a wife named Na Li Ni and a daughter named Bi Nang Ti (Princess of Champa) as well as a son named Bi Nang Na (Ayuningrum, 2017). Quoted from Carita Lasem, the closeness between Lasem and Demak became even tighter with the marriage bond between the Leader of the Demak Kingdom (Raden Patah?) and the daughter of Adipati Lasem Wira Negara and Nyai Ageng Malokah. Indeed, there is no strong supporting evidence regarding this, but the existence of this record can be a small piece connecting the relationship between Demak and Lasem.

The relationship between the Duchy of Lasem, Tuban, and the Demak Kingdom was a kinship relationship as well as a node for Islamic propagation on the North Coast of Java (Unjiya, 2014). Until the end of Demak's rule, Lasem remained an independent duchy, yet very close to the Demak Kingdom. Through a long journey between intrigues and conflicts that occurred in Demak, Sultan Hadiwijaya (Jaka Tingkir) moved the center of Demak to Pajang in the mid-16th century AD (Graaf, 1986). The position of Lasem during the Pajang Kingdom era was no longer an independent duchy. The North Coast of Java area such as Lasem, Gresik, and Tuban had become territories under the Pajang Kingdom's rule. However, there are no definite historical records mentioning how the Pajang Kingdom's conquest of Lasem took place.

One year before the death of Sultan Hadiwijaya (Jaka Tingkir), precisely in 1585, the sultan appointed Raden Teja Bagus Srimpet as the Adipati of Lasem with the title "Tejakusuma" (Unjiya, 2014). Apparently, this selection was also based on the close relationship between Teja Bagus Srimpet and the sultan's daughter. This was seemingly used as a political approach to strengthen relations between Lasem and Pajang. The reason being, after the sultan's passing, Pajang did not yet have a successor candidate to continue his rule because Prince Benawa (A descendant of Hadiwijaya) was not old enough (Graaf, 1986). Therefore, Pajang was led by Arya Pangiri, a leader from Demak who was ordained by Sunan Kudus to rule Pajang. This made Prince Benawa unaccepting, leading him to attack Pajang with the help of Sutawijaya from Mataram (Unjiya, 2014). In 1586, Prince Benawa handed over the rule of Pajang to Mataram as a form of gratitude. Along with this transfer of power, Lasem also became a territory under Mataram's rule. It should be noted that this is what makes Lasem have a city layout similar to other territories under Mataram rule. Entering the 17th century, Lasem experienced political upheaval because in that century the VOC began to stir up Mataram's internal politics.

title: Lasem and Javanese Geopolitics in the 17th-18th Century
content:
Geopolitics theoretically contains two concepts, namely space (geography) and power relations (politics). Space geographically is basically static. Space becomes dynamic because it is not empty; it contains various natural and human resources that can determine the lives of people, welfare, glory, and the fate of a nation (state). Geopolitics is a strategy to control and conquer space as an effort to meet the interests and needs of a nation (state). The desire to control and conquer space is what makes geopolitics important for a country. Economic, technological, social, and cultural changes are consequences of the increasing need for a nation's survival and existence. Therefore, various geostrategies are proposed to control and conquer space (Damayanti, 2005).

In Java, this pattern underlies the process of restoring a hierarchical-concentric geopolitical order according to agrarian primordialism which had been enriched with Indian and Islamic traditions. Geographically, cities in Java can be divided into two parts, namely 'Coastal' and 'Inland' cities. Both Coastal and Inland cities at the beginning of their development had the same structure. Only in subsequent historical developments did Coastal cities have a different structure from Inland cities. This is due to Coastal cities interacting more with foreigners from 'overseas' as a result of advances in shipping and trade. Therefore, the population of Coastal cities was more heterogeneous compared to the relatively homogeneous population of Inland cities. Javanese cities in pre-colonial times essentially had no fixed administrative boundaries. Everything depended on the ruler. A ruler usually resided in the kingdom's or regency's capital. That is why it was so easy for large cities in the past such as Demak, Kota Gede, Kartasura, or Pajang to collapse or even disappear without a trace (Damayanti, 2005).

Javanese cities in pre-colonial times basically followed the Mandala city pattern, as a continuation of city customs in the Hindu-Javanese era. In its implementation, Javanese cities in the past had a city center (core), in the form of the ruler's palace (Keraton or Regency) with a square and other important buildings around it. If an enemy wanted to destroy or conquer the local ruler, the physical symbols of power such as the palace or keraton and its supporting buildings had to be leveled to the ground. Figuratively, the lights had to be turned off first so that the city would then become weak or even die. When the VOC started trading in Batavia, their presence strongly attracted the interest of Chinese immigrants to try their luck in Java, especially in Batavia. They quickly became trading partners. In other words, the presence of the VOC further strengthened the economic motives of Chinese trade abroad. Chinese people engaged in intermediary trade and other trading activities (Jayusman, 2019). This is because the VOC was unable to enter and cooperate with the Javanese society at that time. However, as time went by, the VOC betrayed the wealthy Chinese merchants. The VOC felt that some Chinese merchants were dishonest in sharing profits with the VOC.

With the existing political chaos, it can be ascertained that Java in the 18th century occupied an important position for both local and foreign rulers. If one could control Java, they would control the economy in the Archipelago. Abundant natural resources from both the agricultural and plantation sectors were the main keys to the economy at that time. Especially with the increase in trade routes in Java to all corners of the world, making Java bustling and possessing great potential. The interests binding the colonials in Java were the rice barns, timber, and salt sources around Rembang. For other commodities such as sugarcane and coffee, they were kept regularly supplied. The VOC clearly wanted to control Java. The VOC was not aggressive in attacking local rulers in Java. The VOC in fact lacked the strength and courage to attack the heart of the kingdoms in Java. The VOC pretended to offer an alliance in the political intrigues occurring in Mataram. The VOC affiliated with the legitimate king and punished any rebel who dared to resist. Once the VOC established cooperation with the ruling king, they offered a very strong military force and in return, the king would provide wages in the form of colonial land, which was part of the kingdom itself. Indirectly, the VOC was able to weaken the kingdom's internal power (Remmelink, 2001:7).

Besides dealing with the Javanese, the VOC also monitored the movements of Chinese immigrants. Actually, the Dutch from the beginning already harbored a sentiment against the Chinese. However, in trade politics, the Chinese were needed. Therefore, the Dutch were tossed between two conflicting things; on the one hand, they needed Chinese merchants as intermediaries to the natives for imported goods. But on the other hand, they also often smuggled the people's agricultural produce. Seeing the importance of the trade network between the VOC and immigrant Chinese, and the benefits of the distribution system established by the Chinese, the VOC then offered protection measures against threats from Javanese lords or others. For example, protection to create the conditions needed for the Chinese to extend their trade network (Jayusman, 2019).

In 1740, there was a massive persecution and massacre of the Chinese community in Batavia. This was due to the VOC policy that applied quotas for Chinese immigrants. For those who came illegally, the VOC made them objects of extortion. In 1740, ethnic Chinese fled in droves to Lasem and, by the people of Lasem, they were welcomed by Raden Panji Margana and Oey Ing Kiat. These refugees then united with the Javanese community in Lasem to gather strength to fight back against the VOC. That alliance became the start of a series of wars between the Chinese-Javanese against the VOC and its allies. The peak of the massacre carried out against the ethnic Chinese was when Governor-General Adriaan Valckenier ordered to kill 500 Chinese and behead them (Daradjadi, 2013:36).

The massacre was heard in various regions, igniting the anger of the rebels and resulting in massive attacks against the VOC by the remaining Chinese around Batavia. The battle killed at least 7,000-10,000 Chinese. In the end, the VOC investigated the mastermind behind the rebellion and designated a Chinese Captain named Nie Hoe Kong as the perpetrator and the person who mobilized the masses to rebel. Meanwhile, another fact based on the Dutch perspective, the beginning of the Chinese ethnic massacre occurred when there was a vacancy of the VOC Governor-General and finally Valckenier was decided as the new VOC Governor-General. During his tenure, Dutch commissioner officials enforced discriminatory policies and behaviors against the ethnic Chinese. Chinese people were required to have an identity card. If they did not have one, they would be detained. Furthermore, they were tortured to the point of having their possessions confiscated. This caused rumors among the ethnic Chinese themselves. The VOC, knowing this, took preventive actions against rebellion which made the situation even more heated. Similar resistance also emerged in Java with a series of rebellion events. One of them was the resistance led by Tan Sin Ko around Demak. This resistance emerged not only from the Chinese but also from the Javanese community. In 1741, there were several acts of resistance by the people against the VOC. They managed to push back the VOC several times, one of which was on July 27, 1741, occupying the Rembang area and repelling the VOC troops (Daradjadi, 2013:36).

title: The Yellow War in Lasem in the 18th Century
content: In 1679, Lasem was part of the Mataram Kingdom with the help of Amangkurat II. The Dutch East India Company or Vereenigde Oost-Indische Compagnie (VOC) attacked the Lasem area with the aim of gaining a trade monopoly on the northern coast of Java. Through a quite prolonged war, Lasem was finally conquered. However, this sparked the hatred of the Lasem people towards the Dutch and Mataram rulers who were considered VOC puppets. In 1714, Sultan Pakubuwono I appointed Prince Tejakusuma V (Raden Panji Sasongko) as Adipati of Lasem. Nevertheless, Prince Tejakusuma V disliked Sultan Pakubuwono I up to his successor Sunan Amangkurat IV. Secretly, Tejakusuma assisted Arya Mataram and Prince Purbaya in fighting against the VOC and Sunan Amangkurat IV. After the Mataram rebels diminished in 1721, Tejakusuma resigned as adipati because he disagreed with the close relationship between the sunan and the Dutch, citing the reason of his ears starting to go deaf. A year after Raden Sasongko Tejakusuma V's resignation as Adipati of Lasem, King Pakubuuwono II appointed a descendant of Chinese heritage named Oei Ing Kiat with the title “Tumenggung Widyaningrat” in 1727. Previously, Oei Ing Kiat was the dampo awang (harbormaster) at the Lasem Port, well-known for his loyalty to Tejakusuma V. Like his predecessor, Oei Ing Kiat harbored hatred towards the Dutch because of the trade monopoly and political intervention carried out by the VOC in Mataram (Unjiya, 2014:169).

title: The Angke Massacre of 1740
content:
In 1740, a massive resistance against the VOC was carried out by the Chinese community in Batavia, known as the Angke incident, which claimed thousands of lives. As a result, around 1,000 Chinese from Batavia fled and sought refuge to the east, and some of them arrived in Lasem. The arrival of the Chinese was welcomed by Adipati of Lasem Oei Ing Kiat, who permitted them to establish several new settlements in the Sambong and Narukan areas west of Lasem City. In general, the Batavian Chinese worked as merchants, port employees, and laborers who possessed a hard-working character. As a result, many new workers worked in Lasem, both as port coolies, farm laborers, and mine laborers belonging to the residents. Oei Ing Kiat also employed them in river normalization projects. This was due to the dredging and embankment projects of the Babagan River which was experiencing siltation caused by the Chinese-Batavian fugitives. In addition, they also carried out the widening of the Canal or Kamandung River from Banjar Mlati, Karanggan to the Babagan River door channel so that merchant ships could enter the center of the city. Therefore, Dasun became a bustling port and a trading center (Unjiya, 2014:170).

However, the changes in Lasem did not last long. Upheaval occurred again because the politically strengthening VOC targeted Rembang. The area was highly strategic, located in the middle of western and eastern Java, as well as a trading area supported by abundant forest products in the form of teak wood. Furthermore, Rembang was also considered an important territory for the VOC administration. The VOC then successfully established a regency administration and trade offices in Rembang and Jepara. The VOC's actions were seen as a serious threat and had eroded the territory of the Lasem Duchy. Moreover, Pakubuwono II also called for war against the Dutch colonials in 1741. The Dutch fort in Kartosuro was successfully burned and destroyed, then Sultan Pakubuwono II instructed all regents in the Mataram region to fight against the Dutch. Consequently, Oei Ing Kiat together with Tan Ke Wie and Panji Margono built a militia force along with the people of Lasem with the aim of planning an attack on the VOC barracks in Rembang, Juwana, and Jepara (Atabik, 2016a).

The rebel troops were known as the "Laskar Dampo Awang Lasem". The chosen war strategy was to control the coast or port and then enter the opponent's center of power in the city center. This strategy was considered suitable for the northern coastal areas which they were already familiar with. The activities of the Lasem militia were conducted in secret using codes. The militia also disguised themselves by dressing like Chinese laborers. Oei Ing Kiat also recruited forces from the militias of Arya Mataram and Raden Purbaya who were in the forests of Blora, Purwodadi, and Sukolilo-Pati. After determining the time and making mature preparations to carry out the attack, Laskar Dampo Awang set off towards Rembang, sweeping the coast using junks. The sporadic and unexpected attacks scattered the Rembang VOC legions and they were easily defeated (Unjiya, 2014:173).

title: Battle Locations
content:
After easily defeating the VOC legion in Rembang, Laskar Dampo Awang headed to the VOC headquarters in the ports of Juwana and Jepara. The troops were divided into two; the first troop led by Oei Ing Kiat and Panji Margono headed to Juwana, while the second troop led by Tan Kie Wie headed to Jepara. The attacks on these two areas were carried out simultaneously in order to split the focus of dispatching VOC legion reinforcements from Semarang. In a short time, the soldiers at the Juwana Port were broken and the rest retreated into the city. Juwana at that time had been surrounded from two directions; from the north, Laskar Dampo Awang had occupied the pier, and from the south, militias from Purwodadi, Blora, and Jaken were ready to attack the city. Then a war erupted near the Juwana Square which caused the VOC soldiers to no longer have the freedom to attack using their rifles and cannons, so they could only defend and wait for reinforcements from the Semarang VOC legion. A day later, the reinforcements arrived from the north and rained fire on the city that had been occupied by Laskar Dampo Awang. Coupled with the assistance of Tumenggung Cakraningrat IV's troops bringing forces from Tuban, casualties fell everywhere. Laskar Dampo Awang finally retreated and returned to the sea carrying captured firearms (Unjiya, 2014:174; Purnawibawa, 2020:41).

Meanwhile, the militia led by Tan Ke Wie who carried out the attack in Jepara experienced difficulties. It seemed the VOC had expected the attack so that guarding at the port was tightened. In addition, the presence of the VOC fort on the Jepara coast made this area possess very strong defenses. VOC ships were on standby in Jepara's waters ready to block attacks from the sea. This caused the attack to only take place in the waters around Jepara. Many Dampo Awang militia ships were damaged and destroyed, while the remaining troops could only turn eastward to Mandalika Island to avoid attacks from VOC ships. As a result of the attack from the VOC legion, the militia leader Tan Ke Wie was killed. Thus, the Laskar Dampo Awang attack never even touched the port of Jepara. The remaining troops from both Juwana and Jepara were finally withdrawn by Oei Ing Kiat back to Lasem, disbanding Laskar Dampo Awang. Oei Ing Kiat ordered them to hide all weaponry and war attributes, and immediately return to their respective families, resuming normal life as if nothing had happened. This was done by Oei Ing Kiat to erase their tracks (Unjiya, 2014: 176).

After carrying out the attack, Oei Ing Kiat immortalized the event in a monument inscribed with the names of the victims who died in Chinese characters and hidden in Tambak Batok Mimi, Gedongmulyo, dated 1742. This was done as a memoriam for the Lasem heroes who fell in the battle against the VOC as well as a warning of the Lasem people's resistance.

Afterward, Oei Ing Kiat immediately departed for Mataram and reported the attacks on Rembang, Juwana, and Jepara, explaining that the people of Lasem knew nothing about the attack events (Atabik, 2016a). The attack was carried out by groups of Chinese from various regions who gathered in Lasem without his knowledge. But it seemed Pakubuwono II did not believe him. As a result of the attack event, Lasem City was occupied by the VOC in 1743 AD. Power over Lasem was taken over and Oei Ing Kiat was dismissed from Adipati to Titular Major Tumenggung. Oei Ing Kiat and Panji Margono continued to be heavily monitored, while Chinese people living in villages were forced to move to city areas under special supervision and isolation. The native Javanese were left as they were, still under surveillance (Unjiya, 2014:176).

To run the new government in Lasem, in 1745 VOC Governor-General Van Imhof appointed Suro Adimenggolo III as a puppet official of the Lasem regency based in Tulis, Selopuro, and established a military barracks on Mount Gebang, Warugunung. Imhof also froze the Rembang regency and dismissed the Regent of Rembang Hangabei Hanggojoyo because he was considered involved in the attack carried out by the Lasem militia. However, the administration of the Lasem regency did not proceed according to the VOC's expectations. The hatred and rejection attitude of the Lasem people towards the existence of a VOC-made regency in the Lasem Duchy resulted in non-conducive conditions. Underground movements that had been in the forests and mountains carried out attacks on the Tulis regency and the Gebang barracks. Added to the anger of the Lasem people towards Suro Adimenggolo III, who under the pretext of religion ordered the destruction of historical sites, the demolition of temples, and the forced collection of relics such as inscriptions and heirlooms. Adipati Suro Adimenggolo III even issued a decree stating:

“Whoever is proven to have helped the rioters who attacked the regency and VOC barracks will be sentenced to death; Whoever keeps heirlooms or ancestral inheritance literature must hand them over to the duchy. If caught hiding them, they will be punished with 25 lashes in the square; existing temples in Lasem must be torn down and statues annihilated”

These arrogant actions did not make the people of Lasem afraid, instead, attacks frequently occurred on the Tulis regency and Gebang barracks (Unjiya, 2014:178). Due to the frequent attacks, the Regent then asked the VOC to move the Tulis Lasem regency to Magersari Rembang. The relocation took place in 1748 and resulted in loose supervision of the leaders and the people (Purnawibawa, 2020).

The militias that previously camped and moved around the forests and mountains finally came out and gained the sympathy of the Lasem people. Oei Ing Kiat and Panji Margono also regained their power. The spirit of resistance against the VOC echoed again everywhere. Until an event on Friday, when Kyai Ali Baidhawi delivered a Friday Sermon at the city mosque proclaiming that the war against Dutch tyranny was jihad fi sabilillah (striving in the path of God). Thus, after the fatwa, the number of volunteers joining the struggle forces multiplied. All layers of society, including dancers, fishermen, merchants, nobles, and Islamic students (santri), united into one unity. The Demangs who governed areas far from Lasem such as Pamotan, Sedan, Gada, Kasrema, Badeg, and Ngadem voluntarily sent young men to join the struggle forces. In August 1750, the war broke out. Probably, the Dutch had already known beforehand about a massive movement in Lasem, so reinforcements from nearby legions such as Juwana, Pati, Blora, Jepara, and Tuban were immediately deployed to Rembang.

Nurhajarini et al., (2015) state that the readiness of the Dutch was due to the leaking of information by Pakubuwono II, who sided with the Dutch. The war began on Bonang Beach up to Dasun Port by santris and Chinese people under the command of Oei Ing Kiat against Tuban soldiers brought by Cakraningrat IV. Meanwhile, at Caruban and Gada Beaches, the Lasem Forces under the leadership of Panji Margono fought against the Rembang legion soldiers. This war lasted for three consecutive months. The resistance against the Dutch made the villages and kademangan around Lasem and Rembang feel called to participate in the resistance. On the border of Lasem and Rembang, a battle occurred between forces from Gada, Tireman, Badeg, and Ngadem led by Demang Mlayakusuma against the Dutch legion from Blora. While in the western part of Rembang, the people of Demang Waru, Pengkol, and Babadan joined to attack the Dutch legion reinforcements from Juwana and Pati stationed in Dresi, Kaliori.

The three-month battle certainly claimed the lives of thousands of victims from both sides. All the military legion forces of the VOC from the northern coastal cities were deployed in the war. The people of Lasem fought to the last drop of blood until they were completely unable to resist anymore. With various superior VOC legion weaponry, they were able to break the resistance of the Lasem people. Oei Ing Kiat and Panji Margono also fell in this battle. In early 1751, the resistance of the Lasem People had truly vanished. Lasem City was then reoccupied by the Dutch. The VOC carried out a massive clean-up to remote villages. For people recorded as having resisted, they were sentenced to prison or exiled to overseas islands. Consequently, the city atmosphere became dead as it had just been abandoned by fleeing residents. The series of events of the Lasem people's resistance was then called the “Yellow War” (Unjiya, 2014:181).

Although in the end the resistance of the Lasem people ended in defeat, the fiery spirit of the Lasem community uniting in diversity to fight VOC hegemony at that time became a turning point where various races, ethnicities, nations, and tribes intersected. Uniting to expel the colonizers. After the death of Oei Ing Kiat, the resistance in Lasem was truly extinguished. Lasem was re-controlled by the Dutch, and Oei Ing Kiat's house was occupied by his nephew who was appointed as the Titular Captain of Lasem, while all his ships and boats were confiscated. Raden Panji Margono's Tejakusuman residence was occupied by Mr. Happen, a Dutch controller, in 1751. The Lasem territory was de facto separated from Rembang. Rembang was led by Hangabei Honggojoyo, while Lasem was led by Tumenggung Citrasoma IV. Suro Adimenggolo III was returned to Semarang as he was deemed unsuccessful in preventing the Lasem people's rebellion. In 1780, after the situation in Lasem subsided, the Chinese residents in Babagan, Lasem, founded the Gie Yong Bio Temple to commemorate the merits of the three Lasem rebel figures, namely Tan Kee Wie, Oei Ing Kiat, and Raden Panji Margono.

Meanwhile, the militia led by Tan Ke Wie who carried out the attack in Jepara experienced difficulties. It seemed the VOC had expected the attack so that guarding at the port was tightened. In addition, the presence of the VOC fort on the Jepara coast made this area possess very strong defenses. VOC ships were on standby in Jepara's waters ready to block attacks from the sea. This caused the attack to only take place in the waters around Jepara. Many Dampo Awang militia ships were damaged and destroyed, while the remaining troops could only turn eastward to Mandalika Island to avoid attacks from VOC ships. As a result of the attack from the VOC legion, the militia leader Tan Ke Wie was killed. Thus, the Laskar Dampo Awang attack never even touched the port of Jepara. The remaining troops from both Juwana and Jepara were finally withdrawn by Oei Ing Kiat back to Lasem, disbanding Laskar Dampo Awang. Oei Ing Kiat ordered them to hide all weaponry and war attributes, and immediately return to their respective families, resuming normal life as if nothing had happened. This was done by Oei Ing Kiat to erase their tracks (Unjiya: 176).

The Yellow War in Lasem is one of the historical events that occurred in the Lasem region, Central Java, Indonesia, in the 18th century. This conflict is part of the rivalry between two Chinese groups, namely the Chinese Captain and the wealthy people in Lasem. This war took place between 1731 and 1757 and has left many dark memories for the local population. In the end, the Yellow War in Lasem had a very detrimental impact on the local community. Not only did it damage infrastructure and result in material losses, but it also caused many fatalities among civilians who were not involved in the conflict. Conflicts like this have taught us the importance of resolving disputes peacefully and building mutually beneficial relationships for all parties. As a historical event, the Yellow War in Lasem serves as an important lesson for maintaining peace and harmony among ethnicities and cultures.

Lasem was then known for the diversity of religions embraced, including Islam, Christianity, Confucianism, Buddhism, and Taoism, as well as the well-maintained harmony among religious communities. The architecture of Lasem at that time was influenced by Chinese and Javanese styles, with large houses featuring distinctive Chinese ornaments reflecting prosperity and Chinese cultural influence. In addition, Lasem Culture developed with the emergence of Lasem batik which became known, featuring motifs and colors influenced by Chinese culture. The historical heritage of 17th-century Lasem leaves a cultural wealth that lasts to this day.
